header.text: <instructions>Select the best evidence to support the statement that Johnny has a good memory.</instructions>

text.text: <atomic>I got tired of watching him do it all, so I started digging into the sack myself.</atomic>
<atomic>"Wheee!" I sat down on a dusty chair and stared.</atomic>
"A paperback copy of Gone with the Wind! How'd you know I always wanted one?"
<atomic>"I remembered you sayin' something about it once. And me and you went to see that movie, 'member?</atomic>
<atomic>I thought you could maybe read it out loud and help kill time or something."</atomic>
<atomic>I put the book down reluctantly. I wanted to start it right then.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Prosper laughed. Riccio could always make him laugh, even if he didn't feel like it.</atomic>
<atomic>"Do you sometimes wish you were grown-up?" he asked as they crossed a bridge and looked down at its hazy reflection on the water.</atomic>
<atomic>Riccio shook his head with astonishment. "No. Why? It's great being young. You don't stand out so much and your stomach fills up more quickly."</atomic>
<atomic>He jumped from the bridge onto the street.</atomic>
<atomic>"Children are caterpillars and adults are butterflies. No butterfly ever remembers what it felt like being a caterpillar."</atomic>

contents.text: A relative pronoun introduces a dependent (or relative) clause that describes a noun or pronoun. The five main relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which, and that.
The relative pronouns who and whom give information about people.

header.text: To figure out whether to use who or whom, restate the dependent clause with a personal pronoun. If the clause uses a subject pronoun (he, she, or they), use who. If the clause uses an object pronoun (him, her, or them), use whom.

sentences.text: The woman who lives next door grows tomatoes in her garden.
She lives next door.
Peter, whom you met yesterday, has four younger brothers.
You met him yesterday.

header.text: The relative pronoun that gives necessary information about things. Necessary information narrows down what you're talking about and is not set off by commas.

sentences.text: We walked to a park that has a tire swing.
The information narrows down which park we walked to. It is necessary.

header.text: The relative pronoun which adds unnecessary information about things. This extra information does not narrow down what you're talking about. It is always set off by commas.

sentences.text: We walked to Glendale Park, which has a tire swing.
The information is extra. It does not narrow down which park we walked to.

header.text: The relative pronoun whose shows possession.

contents.text: Emily, whose hair is quite long, likes wearing braids.

header.text: Do not confuse whose with who's. Who's is a contraction for who is or who has. It does not show possession.

sentences.text: Emily, who's quite tall, can reach the top shelf.
Emily, who is quite tall, can reach the top shelf.

sentences.text: She gave me long red silk roses.
The adjectives long, red, and silk all describe the noun roses.

contents.text: When more than one adjective is used, the adjectives usually go in a certain order. This table shows that order.

header.text: A purpose or qualifier is often considered part of the noun. When you put a purpose or qualifier with a noun, the result is similar to a compound word.
<instructions>Put the words in the right order to describe the noun.</instructions>

contents.text: The article a comes first.
The adjective large tells you about the size, so it comes second.
Chocolate is a qualifier, so it comes third.

header.text: The noun doughnut comes last.

contents.text: a large chocolate doughnut
